claims.text: Allowing students to use phones during school can enhance learning by giving them access to educational resources, real-time information, and collaborative tools.
claims.warrant: According to the UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report 2023, integrating technology in education can support personalized learning and improve student engagement when managed appropriately.

claims.text: Permitting phone use in schools can help students develop digital literacy skills that are essential for success in modern society.
claims.warrant: The OECD report on student mobile phone use highlights that responsible technology use in educational settings prepares students for the digital demands of higher education and the workforce.

claims.text: Allowing students to use phones during school increases distraction and negatively impacts learning outcomes.
claims.warrant: The UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report 2023 highlights that mobile phones in classrooms are associated with increased distraction, which can undermine students' ability to focus and learn effectively.

claims.text: Permitting phone use during school can exacerbate inequities among students who have differing access to technology.
claims.warrant: The OECD's review of student technology policies notes that not all students have equal access to smartphones, so allowing their use could widen gaps in participation and educational opportunity.

turns.content: YES, students should be allowed to use phones during school because phones can help with learning. They give students access to educational resources, real-time information, and tools for working together. Research from UNESCO and the OECD shows that using technology in class can make learning more engaging and helps students build important digital skills for the future.

NO, students should not be allowed to use phones during school. Phones in class make it much easier for students to get distracted, which hurts their ability to focus and learn well. The UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report 2023 shows that phones are linked to more distraction and worse learning outcomes. Also, the OECD notes that not every student has a phone, so letting students use them can make things unfair for those who don't.

If the main worry is that phones cause distraction, how do you address the evidence that responsible phone use helps students build digital skills they need for future jobs, as shown in the OECD report?

If phones really help learning, how do you explain the UNESCO report showing that phones in class often distract students and lower their focus? Can you show specific evidence that the benefits outweigh these proven risks?

While the NO side points out that phones can be distracting, the UNESCO report also shows that technology, when managed well, helps students learn in new ways and stay engaged. The OECD source adds that learning to use phones responsibly at school prepares students for real-world digital skills. Allowing phones with clear rules can boost learning and digital literacy without ignoring the risks.

YES says phones help learning and digital skills, but the UNESCO report shows phones mostly distract students and hurt focus. The OECD also warns that letting students use phones can make things unfair for kids who don't have the same devices. These risks are not solved just by hoping students use phones responsibly.

YES, students should be allowed to use phones during school because they can access helpful learning tools and develop digital skills needed for the future. The UNESCO and OECD reports show that, when managed well, phones support personalized learning and prepare students for a digital world.

NO side shows that letting students use phones during school leads to more distractions and makes it harder for everyone to learn, as the UNESCO report explains. The OECD also warns that not all students have phones, so this rule could be unfair. The risks to learning and fairness are too high to allow phones during school.

The NO side provided stronger evidence that allowing phones during school increases distraction and can worsen learning outcomes, as shown in the UNESCO report. While the YES side highlighted potential benefits for learning and digital skills, these were not shown to outweigh the concrete risks of distraction and inequity. Based on the evidence, the burden of proof for changing the current policy was not fully met by the YES side.

categories.name: evidence
categories.note: The pro side cited benefits from UNESCO and OECD about digital skills and engagement, but the con side's evidence from UNESCO directly links phone use to increased distraction and lower learning outcomes, which is more concrete and directly relevant to the classroom environment.

categories.name: practicality
categories.note: Pro argued that responsible management could mitigate risks, but did not provide clear mechanisms for ensuring consistent, effective management across diverse schools. Con's point that distraction is a widespread, hard-to-control problem is more practical given typical school settings.

categories.name: risk
categories.note: Con highlighted specific risks—distraction and inequity—supported by both UNESCO and OECD. Pro acknowledged risks but relied on the assumption that management and rules would be sufficient, without strong evidence that these would reliably prevent harm.

categories.name: fairness
categories.note: Con's argument that allowing phones could worsen inequity for students without access was backed by OECD evidence. Pro did not address how to ensure equal access or prevent new disparities.

categories.name: reversibility
categories.note: Both sides touched on the possibility of managing or adjusting policies, but neither provided detailed arguments about how easily negative effects could be reversed if the policy failed.

summary.headline: Evidence shows allowing phones during school increases distraction and inequity, outweighing potential digital skill benefits.
summary.recommendation: NO—students should not be allowed to use phones during school. The con side provided stronger, more concrete evidence from UNESCO and OECD that phone use leads to increased distraction, lower learning outcomes, and greater inequity. The pro side's arguments about digital skills and engagement did not sufficiently address or outweigh these risks.
